items.stem: Muckrakers furthered the causes of the Progressive movement by
options: organizing grassroots campaigns for political reform at the state level
suing large companies and donating their court awards to Progressive campaigns
staging large, violent protests in support of Progressive goals
alerting the public to the social ills and corporate corruption targeted by Progressives
items.explanation: “Muckrakers” is a term Theodore Roosevelt coined to describe the investigative journalists of his day. They included Ida Tarbell, whose book on Standard Oil revealed corruption in the oil industry and big business in general; Upton Sinclair, whose stomach-turning account of the meatpacking industry drove public outcry for government regulation of food production (the Food and Drug Administration was created as a result of Sinclair’s book The Jungle ); and Lincoln Steffens, whose The Shame of the Cities exposed many Americans to the extent of urban poverty and corruption in urban government. Muckrakers helped fuel the public outcry for government reform, the main goal of the Progressive movement.

items.stem: Keynesian economic theory would assert that
options: government interference in economics for the purpose of remedying a depression will only make matters worse
the way to avoid an economic depression is for people to start saving a high percentage of their incomes as soon as the economy takes a downturn
economic depressions worsen when individuals buy what they cannot comfortably afford
lavish spending during an economic depression should be encouraged
items.explanation: Economist John Maynard Keynes theorized that a depression is the result of a vicious cycle: an economic downturn causes people to become anxious and reluctant to spend money, which leads businesses to fail and the economy to worsen, which leads to even greater anxiety and reluctance to spend money, which exacerbates the economic situation, etc. The way to stop the cycle and improve the economy is, perhaps counterintuitively, for people to spend money freely during times of hardship. The government can facilitate this process by providing its citizens with funds, whether through jobs or handouts, which they will presumably spend and thereby stimulate the economy. Roosevelt’s policies during the Great Depression were based on Keynesian economics.

items.stem: Following the Spanish–American War and the acquisition of territory overseas, in a series of cases known as the Insular Cases, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that
options: natives living on American soil abroad were guaranteed the same rights and privileges as U.S. citizens living within the continental United States
colonial subjects within the American Empire were not entitled to the rights guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution
“the Constitution follows the flag”
Congress must relinquish control of these overseas possessions and honor their right of self-determination
items.explanation: As a result of winning the Spanish–American War in 1898, the United States acquired Guam, Puerto Rico, the Philippines, and for all intents and purposes, Cuba. (Although we had claimed we had no interest in acquiring Cuba and could empathize with its colonial status, having once been a colony ourselves, the Platt Amendment rendered the island a virtual colony of the United States.) The situation in the Philippines created intense debate between business interests that saw the enormous economic benefits to acquiring “stepping stones” to profitable Chinese trade, and those Americans who believed having colonies contradicted our fundamental democratic principles. Once we acquired overseas possessions, a question arose as to the rights and privileges of the Native peoples living within the American Empire. In a series of Supreme Court cases known as the Insular Cases, the Court ruled that the “Constitution did not follow the flag,” and thus, colonial subjects were not entitled to the same rights as U.S. citizens living at home or abroad.

items.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the contents of the Zimmermann telegram, which was intercepted in 1917?
options: Germany offered Mexico an alliance and help regaining land lost in the Mexican Cession if Mexico attacked the United States
A British spy alerted the world to the existence of mass extermination camps in German-held territories.
The United States assured the British that it would join the war in Europe if the war were to continue for another year.
The owner of the Boston Red Sox revealed a plan to sell star player Babe Ruth to the New York Yankees for a large amount of cash.
items.explanation: This is a straight recall question. You either know what the Zimmermann telegram is or you don’t. If you know it, you’re going to get this question right. If you don’t, use Process of Elimination to get rid of anachronistic answers, as in (B), or answers that seem un-AP-like because they don’t reinforce important themes of U.S. history, as in (D). You should know, however, that the Zimmermann telegram was one of the reasons the United States entered World War I.

items.stem: During World War I, the propaganda effort headed by the Committee on Public Information used all of the following techniques to build public support for the war EXCEPT
options: influencing schoolteachers to include lessons on patriotism
mandating a sugar ration of one pound per week
producing prowar posters, buttons, short films, and other media
training people to speak publicly at movie theaters, churches, lodges, and other organizations
items.explanation: The Committee on Public Information was only in existence for three years, but it managed to build, from nothing, a vast propaganda movement that reoriented the American public toward war. This was no small task, seeing as how the United States had maintained a policy and culture of isolationism for the previous century. Choices (A), (C), and (D) were all duties of the CPI, so eliminate them. Rationing of sugar during World War I was a historical fact, but it wasn’t the responsibility of the CPI; therefore, (B) is correct.

items.stem: Wilson’s Fourteen Points plan for peace after World War I included all of the following EXCEPT
options: promotion of universal self-determination
lower tariffs to promote free trade
repayment of all Allied war expenses by Germany
across-the-board arms reductions
items.explanation: In the aftermath of World War I, President Wilson favored a peace that would promote openness in international affairs, free trade, and diplomacy. He also sought universal arms reductions and a mechanism for enforcing world peace, which was to be achieved through the League of Nations. He did not seek a punitive treaty that forced Germany to pay heavy reparations; the European allies, however, insisted. Wilson was able to negotiate very little of his Fourteen Points plan, but he remained optimistic that the League of Nations would eventually broker a fairer postwar peace. Unfortunately, Wilson’s hopes were never realized.

items.stem: All of the following can be seen as clashes between traditional and modern culture during the Post–World War I Era EXCEPT
options: the rise of the Ku Klux Klan
the Teapot Dome Scandal
the Scopes Monkey Trial
the Emergency Quota Act
items.explanation: The Ku Klux Klan evoked the execrable southern traditions of racism and physical intimidation against the modern drive for expanded civil rights. The Scopes Monkey Trial pitted religion against the modern notion of evolution. The Emergency Quota Act was passed to check immigration from non-western European countries; its champions felt the nation’s Western European traditions were threatened by immigrants from Southern Europe, Eastern Europe, South America, and Asia. The Teapot Dome Scandal, on the other hand, was just an example of good old-fashioned political corruption.

items.stem: The stock market crash of 1929 was the result of which of the following? Irresponsible lending by banks and corporations Overspeculation of the value of the stock market Failure of banks to guarantee the security of deposits
options: II only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II, and III
items.explanation: While there were many factors that contributed the stock market crash in October 1929, the leading contributors were apparent overspeculation of the value of the market, which was driven up by lending and irresponsible investing based on the “guarantee” of future profits, a principle known as buying on margin. Much of the lending and support for these transactions was contributed by banks who saw some of the greatest losses and were shuttered during the collapse, leading many Americans to lose their balances in the bank overnight. The FDIC, formed early during Roosevelt’s administration, guaranteed bank deposits backed by the strength of the U.S. government.

items.stem: Which of the following was NOT a New Deal policy?
options: Federal insurance for banks in order to ensure the confidence of depositors
Stricter laws against unionizing in order to prevent loss of income due to strikes
Payments to farmers who agreed to substantially reduce production in order to stabilize prices
Government regulation of the stock market in order to protect investors
items.explanation: Roosevelt adopted a pro-union stance regarding the New Deal, believing that the right to collective bargaining was critical to ensuring decent wages for workers. Americans would have more money to spend if they were adequately paid, and increased spending would benefit the economy.

items.stem: The Nye Commission report of 1936 reinforced American isolationism by
options: revealing unethical profiteering by American munitions companies during World War I
concluding that Germany had no interest in engaging the United States in war
listing the domestic programs that would have to be forfeited if the United States were to increase its overseas commitments
detailing deficiencies in all branches of the U.S. military
items.explanation: Americans were already predisposed to isolationism before they heard the results of the Nye Commission’s investigations. They had been promised that World War I was “the war to end all wars.” Less than 20 years later, Europe was on the verge of another big confrontation. The sentiment in the United States was, “Let them sort this out themselves.” Those feelings were strengthened when the Nye Commission revealed that many American munitions companies had violated an arms embargo in order to arm the nation’s enemies. It further revealed that U.S. banks had lobbied for entry into the war in order to protect more than $2 billion in loans to Britain and its allies. The report left Americans more cynical about the motives of its leaders and less susceptible to calls for intervention overseas.

items.stem: In its Korematsu v. United States (1944) decision, the Supreme Court ruled that
options: the wartime relocation of West Coast Japanese Americans was not unconstitutional
the Japanese government had no legitimate claim to reparations for the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
the U.S. government had violated the Constitution by entering the Korean War
immigration quotas based on race were unconstitutional
items.explanation: Fred Korematsu was among the more than 110,000 Japanese Americans ordered to relocate from the West Coast to internment camps during World War II. Korematsu refused, was arrested, and took his case all the way to the Supreme Court. The Court ruled that the government had not exceeded its power, noting that extraordinary times sometimes call for extraordinary measures; three of the nine justices dissented. History has not judged Roosevelt’s internment policy kindly. In 1998, Fred Korematsu was awarded the Presidential Medal of Honor.
